 1                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

 2   I.       INTRODUCTION

 3            Plaintiff’s lawsuit, which recycles allegations copied-and-pasted across several recent

 4   complaints, is undone by a glaring problem: Even as he urges that Defendant PHH Mortgage

 5   (“PHH”) impermissibly shared information about his website use with third parties for their

 6   marketing purposes, Plaintiff expressly pleads that he contractually authorized exactly that form of

 7   information sharing. That dooms every cause of action, and Plaintiff’s claims independently fail

 8   for a host of additional reasons. The Court should therefore dismiss the Complaint with prejudice.

 9   II.      FACTUAL BACKGROUND

10            A.      Plaintiff Agrees To Contracts That Grant PHH The Right To Share
                      Information About Plaintiff’s Website Use With Non-Affiliated Third Parties
11                    For Their Marketing Purposes.
12            PHH is a “financial services corporation” that issues and “services mortgage loans.” Compl.

13   ¶¶ 2, 17. Its website offers a “calculator” tool that helps visitors assess their financial position and

14   enables visitors to submit loan applications. Id. ¶¶ 2, 46. It also contains a link to another website,

15   libertyreversemortgage.com, where visitors can “learn about and apply for reverse mortgages.” Id.

16            According to the Complaint, Plaintiff entered into several “Privacy Contracts” with PHH

17   that authorized PHH to use information gathered from Plaintiff’s website use.1 Id. ¶ 90. Those

18   contracts—which the Complaint attaches and incorporates by reference—comprise PHH’s

19   “Privacy & Security Policy, California Notice [of] Collection and Privacy Policy/California

20   Consumer Privacy Act Disclos[u]re (‘CCPA Disclosure’), Terms & Conditions, and Privacy

21   Notice.” Id. These contracts repeatedly and comprehensively disclose that PHH may share

22   information it gathers about Plaintiff’s website use with third parties for their marketing purposes.

23            Consumer Privacy Notice. PHH’s Consumer Privacy Notice defines “the reasons” that

24   PHH “chooses to share” website visitors’ “personal information.” Id. ¶ 98. One of the authorized

25   reasons is “[f]or our nonaffiliates to market to you.” Id. The Consumer Privacy Notice defines the

26   term “nonaffiliate” broadly, encompassing all “[c]ompanies not related by common ownership or

27
     1
28       PHH accepts that these documents are binding contracts solely for the purposes of this motion.

 1   control,” whether they are “financial” or “nonfinancial companies.” Id. ¶ 101.

 2          The Complaint thus concedes that the Consumer Privacy Notice “stat[es] that [PHH] ‘can

 3   include’ its Customers’ Personal and Financial Information”—the subject of this lawsuit—in

 4   PHH’s disclosures to “nonaffiliates.” Id. ¶ 102. The Complaint further acknowledges that “the

 5   Consumer Privacy Notice grants PHH the sole discretion to determine whether it will share

 6   Customers’ information with nonaffiliates,” including “whether and what to disclose and when it

 7   discloses it.” Id. Indeed, Plaintiff claims to have “communicate[d] Personal and Financial

 8   Information” to PHH’s website “with the understanding that PHH would not share his Personal and

 9   Financial Information except as agreed in the Privacy Policies.” Id. ¶ 135 (emphasis added).

10          Privacy & Security Policy. PHH’s Privacy & Security Policy says the same thing. It

11   describes how PHH may use any “information”—without limitation—“that We collect about you

12   or that you provide to us.” Id. ¶ 91. And it authorizes PHH to use such information “to work with

13   marketing partners to provide you with products or services that may be of interest to you,”

14   including unaffiliated “retailers and other third parties” who may use the shared information “to

15   market to you.” Id. ¶¶ 91–92. The Privacy & Security Policy also authorizes PHH to share

16   information with “service providers … We use to support our business.” Id. ¶ 92.

17          California Privacy Notice and CCPA Disclosure (California Residents Only). Two

18   other contracts apply specifically to California consumers. First, PHH’s California Privacy Notice

19   confirms that PHH may “share information we collect about you with nonaffiliated third parties …

20   as permitted by law, including, for example, with your consent.” Compl. Ex. D, at 4. The California

21   Privacy Notice then informs “California residents that they have the ‘right[] to restrict the sharing

22   of personal and financial information with our affiliates ... and outside companies we do business

23   with,” Compl. ¶ 106, and provides a mail-in form for consumers wishing to elect a restriction on

24   information sharing, Compl. Ex. D, at 5. Plaintiff does not claim to have restricted sharing.

25          Separately, PHH’s CCPA Disclosure “explains” PHH’s obligations under “the California

26   Consumer Privacy Act.” Compl. ¶ 94. But the CCPA Disclosure has no application here. It

27   expressly “does not apply” to any “consumer or customer of personal, household, or family

28   financial products or services,” including mortgages and reverse mortgages. Compl. Ex. B, at 1.

            B.       PHH Shares Limited Information About How Plaintiff And Other Customers
 1                   Navigate Its Website With Google, Yahoo!, and Microsoft
 2          Plaintiff alleges that PHH shares with Google—and, to a narrower extent, Yahoo! and

 3   Microsoft—select information about how website visitors interact with PHH’s website.2 Although

 4   Plaintiff refers to that information as his “Personal and Financial Information,” e.g. Compl. ¶ 1, it

 5   is far narrower than that. According to the Complaint, PHH purportedly permits these third parties

 6   to access only information about whether a visitor has navigated to a particular webpage or

 7   interacted with a particular field, not what the visitor communicated to PHH. See, e.g., id. ¶¶ 38,

 8   41, 42. There is nothing in the Complaint alleging that PHH shares with Google, Yahoo!, or

 9   Microsoft any substantive information that website visitors input into any field on any page. More

10   specifically:

11          Google only. PHH allegedly shares with Google alone certain information about loan

12   applications, requests for application-related callbacks, and use of PHH’s online loan calculator.

13   Id. ¶¶ 57–80. But that information is notably limited. PHH purportedly informs Google of the bare

14   fact that a website visitor navigated to certain webpages, like those designed to help visitors “learn

15   about getting a loan pre-approval” or access PHH’s loan “calculator.” Id. ¶¶ 59, 78; see id. ¶¶ 60,

16   67–68. PHH also purportedly shares a few data points about how visitors navigate these pages:

17   whether and how far a visitor “scrolled” on the “Get-started” page, id. ¶ 61; whether a visitor started

18   or submitted forms related to an “equity loan” or “callback request,” id. ¶¶ 70, 74–76; and whether

19   a visitor submitted information to the loan calculator, id. ¶¶ 78–80. Critically, though, there is no

20   allegation that PHH shares with Google (or anyone else) any substantive information that a visitor

21   inputs on any of PHH’s webpages. For example, while PHH purportedly discloses that a visitor

22   completed a loan form or used the loan calculator, there is no allegation that it ever shares any of

23   the data that visitors submitted to PHH, like the words entered into a loan application or the numbers

24   entered into a calculator tool.

25

26    The Complaint also alleges that PHH’s website deployed tracking code from a company called
     Hotjar. Compl. ¶¶ 39-40. But it pleads no facts about what data Hotjar’s tracking code collected
27   and never asserts that Hotjar collected any data related to Plaintiff. See id. The Complaint also
     makes two stray references to a “Meta Pixel” but alleges no facts establishing that PHH’s website
28   deployed it, let alone that it collected any data related to Plaintiff. See id. ¶¶ 145, 159.

 2   and Microsoft limited information related to libertyreversemortage.com, a separate website to

 3   which PHH allegedly directs interested visitors. Id. ¶ 81. PHH purportedly shares that a user has

 4   reached that separate website and interacted with its “reverse mortgage calculator.” Id. ¶¶ 82–83,

 5   85–86. Once more, however, Plaintiff does not allege that PHH shares any of the substantive

 6   information that website visitors convey.3

 7          The Complaint asserts that Google, Yahoo!, and Microsoft used information that PHH

 8   shared with them for their own “advertising and marketing purpose.” Id. ¶ 93; see id. ¶ 4. As part

 9   of that marketing, they sometimes “disclosed” the information to so-called “fourth parties who also

10   profited off of it” through their own advertising. Id. ¶ 4. The term “fourth parties” presumably refers

11   to customers of Google, Yahoo!, or Microsoft that did not allegedly interact with PHH, but the

12   Complaint identifies only one such fourth party, alleging that Facebook sometimes purchases data

13   from Google (either directly or indirectly). Id. ¶ 115.

14          C.      PHH Discloses To Its Loan Application Processor Information Necessary To
                    Process Applications
15
            The Complaint separately alleges that PHH uses “Blend, a third-party application
16
     processor … to process its pre-approval loan applications.” Id. ¶ 62. PHH allegedly shares
17
     application information by sending “details that users provide” to Blend’s “self-hosted instance of
18
     the Sentry.io tracker.” Id. For example, when an applicant indicates whether she has “a coborrower”
19
     or owns “any real estate,” PHH allegedly tells Blend whether the applicant answered yes or no. Id.
20
     ¶ 63. Thus, when sharing information with Blend—unlike for Google, Yahoo!, Microsoft, or any
21
     other third party—PHH purportedly discloses the substance of a website visitor’s inputs to PHH’s
22
     website. Of course, that is essential for Blend to process loan applications on PHH’s behalf, and
23
     the Complaint does not allege that Blend used the information for any other purpose.
24

       The limited scope of information allegedly collected and shared here echoes what session replay
26   technology collects about a website visitor. That sort of software likewise determines how website
     visitors navigate a website—including which pages they viewed and which fields they interacted
27   with—without capturing the substance of any information they input. See, e.g., Yoon v. Lululemon
     USA, Inc., 549 F. Supp. 3d 1073, 1082–83 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (session replay software did not collect
28   “content” of website visitor’s communications).

 1          D.      Plaintiff Alleges That PHH’s Information Sharing Is Unlawful

 2          As noted, Plaintiff alleges that PHH expressly disclosed—in contracts to which Plaintiff

 3   “agreed”—that PHH “‘can include’ its Customers’ Personal and Financial Information” in

 4   disclosures to “nonaffiliates,” including “[f]or our nonaffiliates to market to you.” Id. ¶¶ 98, 102,

 5   135. Nonetheless, the Complaint claims that PHH broke the law in nearly a dozen ways when it

 6   shared Plaintiff’s information with third parties for their “marketing purposes.” E.g., id. ¶ 108.

 7   These claims all share the same head-scratching premise: that despite the Complaint’s allegations

 8   to the contrary, PHH somehow fell short of “including in its Privacy Policies that it discloses

 9   Customers’ Personal and Financial Information to Third Parties for their use in their own

10   advertising and marketing,” such that Plaintiff never agreed to that practice. Compl. ¶ 126.

11          If that premise is wrong—that is, if the facts as pled instead establish that Plaintiff did know

12   about and agree to the challenged information sharing—then every claim fails as a matter of law.

13   Claims 1 and 2 (negligence and negligence per se) fail because there was no “unauthorized …

14   disclosure.” Id. ¶¶ 180, 187. Claim 3 (CDAFA, Cal. Penal Code § 502) fails because PHH did not

15   collect information “without permission.” Id. ¶ 208. Claim 4 (UCL, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code

16   §§ 17203–04) fails because PHH did not share information “without” Plaintiff’s “consent.” Id.

17   ¶ 214. Claim 5 (CCPA, Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.115) fails because PHH did not collect, use, or sell

18   Plaintiff’s information “without providing consumers with notice.” Id. ¶ 236. Claim 6 (breach of

19   contract) fails because PHH’s Privacy Contracts never promised to “keep” Plaintiff’s information

20   “confidential.” Id. ¶ 244. Claim 7 (unjust enrichment) fails because PHH never “disclosed”

21   Plaintiff’s information “without [his] consent.” Id. ¶ 249. Claim 9 (breach of confidence) fails

22   because PHH did not share Plaintiff’s information “without notice and consent.” Id. ¶ 267. Claim
